chapter: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
title: Playing leftist rallies with Frankie Newton; Paul Robeson
summary: Collins played three or four well-paid gigs a week at communist meetings with Frankie Newton and Flip Phillips, where Paul Robeson spoke.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: I imagine so, but naturally he wasn't a member, so he couldn't tell who was a card carrier or whatever. I tell you. Speaking of communists I will digress a little bit, but I worked at one time with Frankie Newton. Have you ever heard of Frankie Newton. Frankie Newton was a very fine trumpet player. Frankie Newton and also in this band was a clarinet player by the name of Flip Phillips.
Clarinet. Very fine clarinet player, yeah. And we played nothing with communist dances. And --
How did you get to play the communist
It was work. It didn't make any difference to us if it was communist or fascist.
How did you happen to get on their list?
I don't know. But listen, and at all of these meetings Paul Robeson was there, see, he was the
principal speaker, you know, and we used to do three and four of these gigs a week.

Oh, the pay was beautiful. And I mention that because of Flip Phillips. This is how I first met Flip. We were working with Frankie Newton, another marvelous trumpet player. He's the style of Roy Eldridge. I'm surprised you haven't heard of him.
I may have heard of him, but I don't know his playing. (Inaudible).
